title: How does Norfolk's Zoning Ordinance decide what's allowed where, and how does a Conditional Use Permit work?
summary: General rules from the City's official Zoning Ordinance: how to read a use table (P, C, P/C, blank; unlisted uses are prohibited; an overlay district's column can allow or prohibit a use whatever the base district says), the standards a Conditional Use Permit is judged by and keeps being held to, when an approved permit lapses, what the Official Zoning Map decides, and how to get a written interpretation. Which district an address is in comes from the City's open-data map layers (parcel_inventory), which Siren treats as a guide, not a legal determination; whether a particular use is allowed there needs that use's row, read in the district's column (and any overlay's column), from the ordinance itself. Who hears and decides a Conditional Use Permit (a Planning Commission hearing, then City Council) is in the norfolk-zoning-restaurant-ghent case file.

findings.claim: The ordinance's use tables say in which zoning districts each use is allowed and what kind of permit or review it needs (§3.1.4).

source.title: City of Norfolk Zoning Ordinance (official approved PDF, adopted January 23, 2018, updated October 13, 2026)

what_would_help.text: To see whether a use is allowed at an address, find its district first, then read the use's row in that district's column of the use table, and any overlay district's column: P allowed, C needs a Conditional Use Permit, P/C may need one depending on the use's performance standards; blank or unlisted means it can't be newly established there unless an overlay column allows it. Whether a proposed use fits a listed one is the Zoning Administrator's interpretation (§2.4.17), and an existing nonconforming use may be allowed to continue (§6.2.1).

For a binding answer about one property, a landowner, resident or business owner can ask the Zoning Administrator for a written interpretation (§2.3.8); if it isn't appealed in time, it becomes final.

If a Conditional Use Permit is approved, and unless the permit sets other terms, start construction or the use within 12 months, or ask the Zoning Administrator before it expires for an extension (up to six months, for good cause, if the use complies with the ordinance); a longer one needs City Council.

records_to_request: Written interpretations of the Zoning Ordinance issued by the Zoning Administrator under §2.3.8 in the last two years (Department of City Planning).
The list of Conditional Use Permits approved, denied and withdrawn by City Council in the last two years, with ordinance numbers (City Clerk).
pending: The use tables' individual rows (for example, whether a given use is P, C or blank in a given district): a cell in a table column can't be quoted exactly from the PDF's text, so no row is a finding yet. Tables 3.2.12 (residential), 3.3.9 (commercial), 3.4.11 (downtown), 3.5.7 (industrial), 3.6.11 (historic and cultural conservation), 3.7.13 (special purpose) and 3.9.23 (overlay districts) hold them; ordinance_lookup reads the sections.

The Official Zoning Map is the final authority (§1.6.1), and the City's open-data Zoning layer that parcel_inventory reads is not it; whether and how often the layer is reconciled with the official map isn't stated in the ordinance.
How often Council approves or denies Conditional Use Permits: that would need the Council's legislation records, counted, not the ordinance.
Other ways a Conditional Use Permit ends, also in §2.4.8 (an expiration date set in the approval; a later permit for the same use on the same site revoking the earlier one), are not yet findings.

Limits beyond the use table are not yet findings: conditional rezoning (§2.4.4, conditions a landowner offers), nonconforming uses (§6.2.1), and the Norfolk Historic Landmark exception (§2.4.7, a Conditional Use Permit route for listed uses in landmark buildings outside the HC and HO districts).
